To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the enamine of the carbanionic thiamin cofactors in pyruvatedehydrogenase is not formed, but instead a tautomeric equilibration between the carbanion and the ketone is observed.
a tautomeric carbanion/keto equilibrium exists in the active site of pyruvate decarboxylase.
the carbanion of the thiamidyl cation intermediate is in equilibrium with the ketone of the thiamine cation, and that this equilibrium is important for the catalytic mechanism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms of enzymes, which catalyze redox-coupling chemical reactions.
the elucidation of the mechanism of the enzyme pyruvate:quinone oxidoreductase, which catalyzes the oxidation of pyruvate to acetyl phosphate.
the elucidation of the catalytic mechanisms of enzymes, which are involved in the metabolism of carbohydrates and other small molecules.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the thiamin diphosphates in thiamin oxidase are not enamines but rather carbanions, which are in tautomeric equilibrium with the ketones.
thiamin enzymes are not enamines, and thiamin diphosphates are not enamines either.
this enzyme is not only an oxidase but also a carbanionase, and that the carbanion is the true substrate of the reaction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
thiamin is a versatile coenzyme, which is capable of sampling between two tautomeric states of the acyl-carbanion equivalent.
we now understand how the enzyme catalyzes a two-step, redox-couple acyl transfer from the carbanion to phosphate.
we now know the structure of the carbanionic intermediate in a thiamin-dependent enzyme and that we can explain the mechanism of the enzyme-catalysed acyl transfer to water and phosphate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
thiamin enzymes have the potential to be much more versatile than we have appreciated until now.
thiamin diphosphates, in addition to their well-known ability to stabilize carbanions by π-delocalization, can stabilize them by a novel, alternative mechanism.
the thiamin diphospate cofactor in the pyruvate-oxidizing pyruvate:flavin oxidoreductase (PFO) does not form an enamine but instead exists in equilibrium between the carbanion and the keto tautomers.
